newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland to party with Clinton, then start NATO work.
newsitem.headline: Poland to party with Clinton, then start NATO work.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton joins Poles on Thursday in an exuberant Warsaw street party to fete their country's invitation to join NATO.

He and Polish President Alexander Kwasniewski were to address thousands of people celebrating in Warsaw's Old Town the decision of NATO on Wednesday to bring Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary into membership talks.

Poland, swallowed by its neighbours from the late 18th to early 20th centuries, ravaged by German occupiers in World War Two, then left by wartime allies to four decades of Soviet-imposed communist rule until 1989, has reason for joy.

"This day is among the most important in the last three centuries of Polish history, because fate has not treated Poland kindly for 300 years", wrote Gazeta Wyborcza daily's editor Adam Michnik, who spent years in communist jails.
But Poland has much to do before clinching its planned admission to the world's strongest defence alliance in 1999, a step backed by 90 percent of its people.
It has to win ratification from all 16 NATO member parliaments and sees the chief hurdle in 100 U.S. senators, two thirds of whom must give their approval a year from now.

Some U.S. commentators fear the entry to NATO of Poland, with its 38 million people and a 220,000-strong army, may antagonise Russia or undermine its democrats -- a view Moscow may seek to reinforce despite the new NATO-Russia charter.
They also worry over extra spending and military commitments Polish entry may entail for the United States.
Clinton will discuss with Kwasniewski and other officials how to address these challenges, while Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will meet Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati.

The celebrations with jazz bands and balloons, dubbed the Day of Eagles after the two countries' symbols, had a message for the U.S. public via television that Poland will contribute eagerly to the pact.

"This will show American opinion instantly that this is something important and historic and must be carried through, because in the United States there are sceptics and even opponents of enlarging NATO," Kwasniewski told Polish radio.
The TV images of Warsaw, rebuilt from destruction by the Nazis, would carry an emotional impact, he said last month.
He said many Americans including Clinton felt a moral debt to Poland, which U.S. and British leaders reluctantly left to Soviet influence in 1945 and which fought so hard for liberty.
Posters for the party were emblazoned with the old Polish wish -- so often disappointed -- "Nothing must be decided about us without us."
Once Clinton leaves on Friday for Bucharest to reassure Romania and other former communist states left out of the first wave of new members, Poland will get back to NATO work.

This week it will name a negotiator for August-September talks with NATO on military adjustments to achieve compatibility with alliance standatds -- moves likely to cost up to $3 billion over 15 years.

Poland must finish drafting a costly military-industrial plan to modernise its forces so it can contribute more fully to NATO operations and defend itself without harming its vital economic growth, expected to reach some six percent this year.

Poland also aims to work on links with Russia to show it will not be a source of tension with its old foe and will keep building military and political ties with Ukraine and other neighbours which it sees as its special role within NATO.
Polish officials claim credit for stressing the importance of independent Ukraine and say this contributed to the special NATO-Ukraine pact signed in Madrid on Wednesday.

All of this coincides with campaigning for September 21 general elections which will pit the co-ruling social democratic party of ex-communists against a rightist alliance led by the Solidarity trade union.
